# Equality in the effective cap-count bound
`candidate 07f233a26b321ff2`, currently in
independent audit, and the independently audited ordinary cap-profile
and strict open-cover theorems. It is not an OC proof.

## 1. Equality for r+1 caps of a log-concave density

Let r>=2 and let f be an integrable log-concave density on R^r with
full-dimensional positive support and mass V>0. Let m=r+1 closed
halfspaces H_i cover its positive support, and let A_i=integral_(H_i)f.
For alpha>0 the audited hereditary-depth/distal-trimming argument gives

    sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/Gamma_r >= V.             (1)

**Theorem.** Equality holds in (1) if and only if all A_i=alpha=Gamma_r V,
and there are a point y and a centroid-centered r-simplex T such that:

* f(y+x)=F(p_T(x)) almost everywhere, where F is a log-concave,
  nonincreasing radial profile of positive finite integral;
* the H_i are exactly the r+1 canonical vertex halfspaces of T through y,
  with no repetition.

Here a canonical vertex halfspace has boundary through the centroid and
parallel to the opposite simplex facet, retaining that vertex. It is a
halfspace of the entire space, independent of the radial scale of T.

### Proof

Sufficiency follows from polar integration: these caps cover all space,
and each has the same fraction Gamma_r as on the uniform simplex.

For necessity, remove from each H_i with A_i>alpha its distal parallel
cap of original f-mass A_i-alpha. Denote the retained intersection by D
and the density f'=f 1_D, of mass V'. Nonverticality here is ordinary
nonzero normals; all hyperplane boundaries are Lebesgue null. Since f
is positive on its support interior, the needed positive-tail quantiles
exist at finite thresholds. Its density has zero mass on any boundary
hyperplane. We have

    V' >= V-sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+,  and integral_(H_i) f'<=alpha.

If (1) is equality, these facts and the hereditary Gamma_r bound force

    V'=alpha/Gamma_r,  D(f')=Gamma_r,
    V'=V-sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+.                            (2)

In particular f' has positive mass and full-dimensional convex support.
The root equality theorem for log-concave densities now gives
f'(y+x)=F(p_T(x)) for a centroid-centered simplex T and a deepest point y
in the interior of its positive support.

Any original cap containing y has f'-mass at most alpha and through-y
mass at least alpha. It cannot contain y strictly: then the intervening
slab in a ball of positive density about y has positive mass. Thus its
boundary passes through y and its mass is alpha. Angular preservation
for the gauge profile and the ordinary simplex equality case show that
it is a canonical vertex cap of T. Caps not containing y miss an entire
neighborhood of y. Any proper subset of the r+1 canonical vertex caps
fails to cover every neighborhood of y: their normals are linearly
independent, so some direction has negative scalar product with all of
them. Since there are only r+1 caps altogether and they cover the support
near y, they must all be the distinct canonical caps through y.

It remains to exclude a positive distal removal. Suppose A_i>alpha for
some i, with retained threshold t_i and original canonical threshold b_i.
Because the original mass in the band b_i<=ell_i<=t_i is alpha>0,
t_i>b_i=ell_i(y). Equality in the last part of (2) says that the removed
distal caps have pairwise intersection of f-mass zero. Thus in the
positive-mass distal piece for i there is a point x in the original
support interior satisfying ell_i(x)>t_i and all other genuinely
trimmed inequalities strictly. Boundary hyperplanes are null, so such
an x can be chosen away from them. At y, every genuinely trimmed
inequality is strict as well. The segment from y to x crosses
ell_i=t_i inside the original support and strictly inside every other
retained inequality. A relative neighborhood of that crossing point
in ell_i=t_i is therefore a facet patch of the support closure of f'.

On the other hand, the gauge-profile support closure is either all
R^r, or a positive homothetic copy of T centered at y. The presence of
one finite upper cut excludes the former, since the cut bounds a ray
from y. In a simplex every canonical vertex-cap normal exposes only
its corresponding vertex. It cannot expose a facet patch of dimension
r-1>=1. This contradiction rules out every positive removal. Equation
(2) now gives V=alpha/Gamma_r, and all original caps, already identified
as canonical, have mass alpha. The original density equals f' almost
everywhere, proving the theorem.

The proof explains why r=1 is excluded: a canonical vertex direction
of an interval exposes a facet (an endpoint), so unequal two-cap
partitions can attain the corresponding union bound.

## 2. Equality for few caps in an arbitrary ordinary dimension

Let K be a convex body of dimension D, with volume V>0. Let 3<=m<=D+1
closed halfspaces H_1,...,H_m cover K. Set r=m-1 and let A_i be their
ordinary D-volumes. For alpha>0 the effective cap-count theorem gives

    sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/Gamma_r >= V.             (3)

**Corollary.** Equality in (3) holds precisely under these conditions:

1. The cap normals have rank exactly r=m-1.
2. Projecting onto their span, the marginal density of uniform volume on
   K is a log-concave gauge profile of a centroid-centered r-simplex,
   about some projected point y.
3. The projected caps are the r+1 distinct canonical vertex halfspaces
   through y, and alpha=Gamma_r V (hence every A_i=alpha).

Projection here is ordinary integration over real orthogonal fibers;
no lattice or sampled measure is being transformed.

To prove necessity, first suppose the cover has a proper subcover of
j<m caps. Its effective dimension min(D,j-1) is strictly less than r.
Its proved profile inequality, together with nonnegativity of the extra
positive parts, makes (3) strict because alpha>0 and Gamma_{j-1}>Gamma_r.
For j=1 use Gamma_0=1, with the same strict comparison. Thus equality
requires an inclusion-minimal m-cap cover.

If the normal rank rho<r, the log-concave marginal in dimension rho has
hereditary Gamma_rho depth. Its profile inequality again makes (3)
strict. If the rank is m=r+1, the independently audited strict
independent-normal profile theorem makes (3) strict: the projective
margins give a genuine open cover, retaining every alpha>0. The only
remaining rank is r. Ordinary projection gives a full-dimensional
log-concave marginal in that dimension and preserves the cap masses.
Apply Section 1 to obtain all the asserted structure. Conversely those
conditions give equality by the angular identity for the profile.

In particular the sharp three-cap coefficient3/4 in every D>=2 can
have equality only for rank-two normals and a triangular gauge-profile
marginal. Rank-three covers have strict inequality. In the case m=D+1,
the marginal is simply uniform volume on K, so the conclusion reduces
to the already audited simplex/canonical-cap rigidity theorem.

No equality or stability classification for m>D+1 is asserted here.
Additional zero or subthreshold caps can occur there, and must not be
excluded by extrapolating the minimal-cover argument.
